title: Lebanon: Cedars, Meeting House, County Seat
summary: Lebanon, the Marion County seat, grew from a settlement around Hardin's Creek Meeting House, a Presbyterian congregation founded in 1789.
bodyMarkdown:
Lebanon, the Marion County seat in central Kentucky, grew from a frontier congregation whose settlers, Grokipedia notes, arrived amid Native resistance. The town's name, its county and its Civil War scars all trace back to that early period.

## A meeting house on Hardin's Creek

The [ExploreKYHistory entry on Lebanon](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/259), which follows state historical marker #867, says the town grew from a settlement around Hardin's Creek Meeting House. Settlers from Virginia founded that Presbyterian congregation in 1789.

The [Grokipedia entry on Lebanon](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lebanon,_Kentucky) adds earlier names. It says surveyors James and Jacob Sandusky explored the area and that Charles and Edward Beavin set up an outpost on Hardin's Creek in 1779. Catholic families from Maryland also settled nearby in the 1780s.

## Cedars and a county seat

Lebanon was formally established in 1814 and incorporated the next year. Grokipedia credits Benedict Spalding and surveyor John Handley with laying out its streets. The name supposedly came from the many cedar trees, which recalled the cedars of biblical Lebanon.

The town sat first in Nelson County, then in Washington County after 1792. When Marion County was created from Washington County in 1834, Lebanon became its seat. The county was named for Francis Marion, the South Carolina Revolutionary War officer known as the "Swamp Fox."

## Railroad and war

A spur of the Louisville and Nashville Railroad reached Lebanon in 1857, paid for by subscriptions from county residents. The line tied local farms to markets north and south. It also made the town a target in the Civil War.

ExploreKYHistory says Union general George Thomas used Lebanon as a base for his Mill Springs campaign in early 1862. Confederates occupied the town for nearly a month that fall, and John Hunt Morgan's raiders came three times. At the Battle of Lebanon on July 5, 1863, many buildings burned.

Grokipedia says the county clerk's office was among them, burned with all county records. From 1864 to 1865 the town was also a recruiting station for United States Colored Troops.

## Kentucky today

Lebanon remains the Marion County seat, with about 6,300 residents at the 2020 census. ExploreKYHistory says the railroad helped it recover after the war, and the town later marketed itself as a center of industry. Today Lebanon and Marion County promote heritage tourism, including the area's deep Catholic roots.
